question: Inhibin: a new circulating marker of hydatidiform mole?
answer: Serum inhibin is elevated in patients with complete hydatidiform mole before evacuation (median 8.3 U/ml vs 2.8 U/ml in normal pregnancy) and falls significantly after evacuation to follicular-phase levels, supporting its use as a circulating marker. Molar tissue contains high concentrations of inhibin (median cytosol 578 U/ml), consistent with a trophoblastic source of the circulating hormone. In a small series of 17 patients with hydatidiform mole, invasive mole or choriocarcinoma, inhibin A was raised in 10/17 and inhibin B in 4/17; inhibin A tracked HCG during chemotherapy and normalized faster than HCG in some patients, while inhibin B did not correlate with HCGbeta. None of the four patients with post-evacuation serum inhibin of 0.4 U/ml or less developed persistent trophoblastic disease, suggesting possible prognostic value.

question: Discharging patients earlier from Winnipeg hospitals: does it adversely affect quality of care?
answer: In Winnipeg's seven large acute care hospitals, length of stay fell significantly from 1989-90 to 1992-93 (11.1% for AMI to 22.0% for bronchitis/asthma) without a consistent rise in 30-day readmission rates for AMI, bronchitis/asthma, or TURP. Physician visits within 30 days after discharge changed little (a slight rise for AMI in the first year, a slight fall for bronchitis/asthma), and hospital-level length of stay was not significantly correlated with readmission rates or physician visits in 1992-93. The only adverse signal in the Winnipeg data was a significant increase in readmissions for uterine or adnexal procedures between the first and second year, which then stayed constant over the next three years. Evidence from outside Winnipeg is consistent: shorter discharge timing was not linked to higher rehospitalization or late mortality after coronary bypass surgery in Canada, and short stays were not linked to higher readmission among Medicare patients.

question: Transesophageal echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular function in brain-dead patients: are marginally acceptable hearts suitable for transplantation?
answer: In a prospective study of 55 potential brain-dead donors assessed by TEE, hearts with marginal left ventricular function (fractional area change <50%) were successfully transplanted: 9 of the 36 successful transplants came from such donors. Actuarial survival of recipients of hearts with FAC <50% was not significantly different from that of recipients of hearts with FAC >50% (86.2% vs 64.6% at 1 and 2 years, p = NS), and fractional area change improved from 51% to 57% in 18 hearts assessed in both donors and recipients. Two of the four recipient deaths were from ventricular dysfunction (one right, one left) in donors with FAC <50%, while the other two deaths were from hemorrhage in donors with FAC >50%.

question: Vertical lines in distal esophageal mucosa (VLEM): a true endoscopic manifestation of esophagitis in children?
answer: In a retrospective review of pediatric esophageal biopsies, VLEM as the only mucosal abnormality was almost always associated with histologic abnormality (histology normal in only 1 of 41 biopsies, 2.4%, versus 57.5% in endoscopically normal mucosa), supporting VLEM as a true endoscopic sign of esophagitis. question: Are head and neck specific quality of life measures necessary?
answer: Head and neck-specific measures appear necessary: in 55 head and neck cancer patients, the Head&Neck Survey correlated more strongly with other specific measures than with a general health measure. Eating/swallowing and speech/communication domains were not well correlated with general health domains, and appearance was not fully reflected by any other domain, so general QOL instruments miss these areas. Head and neck pain was highly correlated with general bodily pain (0.88), suggesting that the pain domain is the one area well captured by a general measure.

question: Does the SCL 90-R obsessive-compulsive dimension identify cognitive impairments?
answer: In 19 adults with malignant brain tumors, the SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was not related to objective measures of attention, verbal memory, or age, so it did not identify objectively measured cognitive impairment. question: Hypotension in patients with coronary disease: can profound hypotensive events cause myocardial ischaemic events?
answer: In an observational study of 25 patients with ischaemic heart disease on hypotensive drugs, ST-segment ischaemic events were significantly associated with preceding ambulatory hypotensive events (chi2 = 40.2, p<0.0001), with 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events occurring in 8 patients. Thirteen of the 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events were preceded by a fall in diastolic pressure, while six were preceded by a fall in systolic pressure. question: Fatigue in primary Sjögren's syndrome: is there a link with the fibromyalgia syndrome?
answer: Fatigue was common in primary Sjögren's syndrome (68%), and fibromyalgia was present in 12% of pSS patients, a higher rate than in lupus controls (5%), suggesting an association between fatigue in pSS and fibromyalgia. question: Is alexithymia a risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of internal medicine outpatients, those with medically unexplained physical symptoms (169 of 321) were not overall more alexithymic than those with explained symptoms, so alexithymia was not shown to be a risk factor. question: Is semi-closed endarterectomy of the superficial femoral artery combined with a short venous bypass in case of insufficient venous material an acceptable alternative for limb-threatening ischemia?
answer: In 30 patients with critical leg ischemia and insufficient venous material, semiclosed SFA endarterectomy combined with a short venous bypass gave a cumulative primary patency of 60.3% at 1 year and 48.4% at 3 years. question: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
answer: In a prospective study of 224 IVF patients, baseline antral follicle count >6 was associated with a much higher clinical pregnancy rate than count ≤6 (51% vs 19%), and this difference persisted after controlling for age and basal FSH, suggesting antral follicle assessment adds predictive information beyond them. Cancellation rate was also much higher with baseline antral follicles ≤6 than >6 (33% vs 1%), though it also rose with advancing maternal age and elevated basal FSH. question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome in children with malignancy--can we predict outcome?
answer: In a retrospective series of 17 children with malignancy and ARDS on mechanical ventilation, only 6 (35.3%) survived, and respiratory variables predicted outcome: peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP and ventilation index distinguished survivors from non-survivors by day 3. question: Does tranexamic acid reduce desmopressin-induced hyperfibrinolysis?
answer: In a randomized trial of 100 CABG patients, adding tranexamic acid to desmopressin reduced fibrinolysis-related markers and bleeding compared with desmopressin alone: fibrin split products were lower (13.5 vs 21.2 ng/mL) and fibrinogen higher (167 vs 113 mg/dL). question: Is specialty care associated with improved survival of patients with congestive heart failure?
answer: In a large VA retrospective cohort of CHF patients, those with combined general medicine and cardiology follow-up had the best 1-year survival; relative to that group, adjusted risk of death was 1.26 for general medicine only and 1.48 for neither clinic, while cardiology-only (1.12, CI 0.94-1.34) was not significantly different. question: Locoregional opening of the rodent blood-brain barrier for paclitaxel using Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy: a new concept of adjuvant glioma therapy?
answer: In rats, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermotherapy (LITT) opened the blood-brain barrier locoregionally, shown by extravasation of Evans blue, C3C, fibrinogen and IgM, and HPLC confirmed paclitaxel passage across the disrupted barrier into brain tissue. Indirectly, in a rat mammary tumor model, combining thermal ablation (RF) with liposomal paclitaxel increased intratumoral paclitaxel accumulation and tumor coagulation compared with paclitaxel alone, consistent with heat-based enhancement of paclitaxel delivery.

question: Can progression of valvar aortic stenosis be predicted accurately?
answer: In a cohort of 169 men and 88 women with aortic stenosis studied at two catheterizations, progression was found to be sufficiently predictable for clinical purposes, depending on the degree of valvar calcification and the initial hemodynamic severity (transaortic gradient or valve area). Specific thresholds were proposed: if valve area falls below 0.75 cm2 with no calcification, 0.8 with calcification grade I, 0.9 with grade II, or 1.0 with grade III, surgery is probably needed in the following years.

question: Sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma: is it clinically meaningful?
answer: In a Danish long-term cohort of children with cerebellar astrocytoma, histological sub-classification did not provide meaningful prognostic information: survival did not differ between pilocytic and fibrillary astrocytoma, and the Kernohan and WHO systems had no predictive value. question: Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis--is it the same disease as adult ankylosing spondylitis?

question: Is eligibility for a chemotherapy protocol a good prognostic factor for invasive bladder cancer after radical cystectomy?
answer: In a matched comparison after radical cystectomy, patients eligible for and entered into an adjuvant chemotherapy protocol had markedly better outcomes than matched and remaining non-protocol patients, with median overall survival of 76.3 vs 52.1 vs 20.3 months. question: Is gastric electrical stimulation superior to standard pharmacologic therapy in improving GI symptoms, healthcare resources, and long-term health care benefits?
answer: In a 3-year comparison of gastroparesis patients, gastric electrical stimulation (GES) produced more sustained symptom improvement over 36 months than intensive medical therapy (F = 3.03, P<0.017). question: Can bedside assessment reliably exclude aspiration following acute stroke?

question: Is laparoscopic adrenalectomy safe and effective for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm?

question: Are adult body circumferences associated with height?
answer: In NHANES III adults, waist and hip circumferences scaled significantly with height after adjustment for age and race (powers about 0.76 and 0.45 in men, 0.80 and 0.53 in women, all P<0.001), with increments of 0.2 to 0.5 cm per cm of height. question: Does minimal access major surgery in the newborn hurt less?

question: Does a colonoscopy after acute diverticulitis affect its management?
answer: In a retrospective review of 220 patients with CT-confirmed acute diverticulitis, early colonoscopy (4-6 weeks after discharge) in 100 patients found no colonic malignancy and produced no new or different diagnosis, suggesting it did not change management. question: Is the determination of specific IgE against components using ISAC 112 a reproducible technique?
answer: ISAC 112 specific IgE determination showed largely good reproducibility: intra- and inter-assay agreement was very good for 94 allergens and good for one. question: Clinical identifiers for early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis: are we seeing the real picture?
answer: In a cross-sectional validation of 8 Delphi-derived clinical identifiers in 64 patients with early-stage adhesive capsulitis, only 25% (16) had a positive anesthetic response, suggesting the proposed identifiers do not reliably capture the true early-stage picture. question: Does the sex of acute stroke patients influence the effectiveness of rt-PA?
answer: In 369 rt-PA-treated stroke patients with acute TCD, men and women did not differ in complete, partial, or no recanalization (p=0.6), and regression showed no sex difference in recanalization, time to recanalization, or 3-month outcome. question: Is there any relation between cervical cord plaques and discopathy in patients with multiple sclerosis?
answer: In a retrospective study of 536 MS patients, cervical cord plaques coincided with the site of cervical discopathy in 148 of 214 patients (69.1%) who had both findings. question: Do emergency ultrasound fellowship programs impact emergency medicine residents' ultrasound education?
answer: Residents in EM programs with EUS fellowships reported performing more ultrasound scans than residents in programs without fellowships (P = .04). question: Is scintigraphy a guideline method in determining amputation levels in diabetic foot?
answer: In a 30-patient diabetic foot series, 3-phase bone scintigraphy was used to mark the amputation level (most distal perfused region), together with Doppler ultrasound and intraoperative inspection, so it was applied as a guide to level selection. question: HIF1A as a major vascular endothelial growth factor regulator: do its polymorphisms have an association with age-related macular degeneration?
answer: No statistically significant difference in the distribution of HIF1A polymorphisms (rs11549465 and rs11549467) emerged between 87 AMD patients and 80 healthy controls, so no association was found. question: May student examiners be reasonable substitute examiners for faculty in an undergraduate OSCE on medical emergencies?
answer: In a randomized comparison of 207 third-year students in an emergency medicine OSCE, students examined by student examiners scored significantly higher on three stations (TM, AM, OE) and on overall OSCE score, while faculty examiners gave a higher score on one station (PE); effect sizes were mostly small, suggesting student examiners are a reasonable substitute. question: Is vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency related to the development of osteochondritis dissecans?
answer: In a prospective pilot study of 23 patients with stage III/IV osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions, 18 had a distinct vitamin D3 deficiency and 2 were insufficient, so most patients had low vitamin D, supporting a possible contributing role in OCD development.

question: Does radiotherapy of the primary rectal cancer affect prognosis after pelvic exenteration for recurrent rectal cancer?
answer: In a retrospective review of 87 patients undergoing pelvic exenteration for locally recurrent rectal cancer, prior radiotherapy for the primary tumour was associated with worse outcomes, including lower disease-free survival (p = 0.022) and lower clear resection margin rates (63% vs 87%). question: Rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane: is partial prostatectomy oncologically adequate?
answer: Partial prostatectomy after preoperative chemoradiotherapy gave a free anterior CRM in all cases in this series of rectal cancers threatening or affecting the prostatic plane, so it appears oncologically adequate. Margin status matters for outcome in locally advanced rectal cancer after chemoradiotherapy: local recurrence was 10% with R0 resection versus 62% with R1-R2 resection, and 3-year overall survival was 64% versus 25%.

question: Living in an urban environment and non-communicable disease risk in Thailand: Does timing matter?
answer: In a Thai cross-sectional survey of hospital health care workers, both early-life urban exposure and the proportion of life years spent in urban areas were independently associated with increases in all behavioral and physiological NCD risk factors studied. question: Literacy after cerebral hemispherectomy: Can the isolated right hemisphere read?
answer: In seven individuals who had left hemispherectomy for seizures linked to perinatal infarct, about 60% developed word reading and paragraph reading in the average range, indicating the isolated right hemisphere can support reading. question: Preparing patients at high risk of falls for discharge home after rehabilitation: Do we meet the guidelines?
answer: Guidelines were not fully met: in a retrospective audit of 50 high-falls-risk patients discharged home after inpatient rehabilitation, discharge documentation correctly identified falls risk for only nine patients. question: MR Diagnosis of Bone Metastases at 1.5 T and 3 T: Can STIR Imaging Be Omitted?

question: Does cup-cage reconstruction with oversized cups provide initial stability in THA for osteoporotic acetabular fractures?
answer: In a prospective radiostereometric study of 10 elderly patients with acute acetabular fractures, THA with an oversized cup and cup-cage achieved acceptable initial stability in most cases, with median 1-year proximal migration of 0.83 mm and sagittal rotation of 1.3°, within limits that predict later loosening in primary THA. question: Utility of unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI in children with sickle cell disease -- can it differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis?

question: Are financial incentives cost-effective to support smoking cessation during pregnancy?
answer: In a cost-effectiveness analysis based on a Phase II RCT of 612 pregnant women in Glasgow, financial incentives of up to £400 had an incremental cost of £1127 per cotinine-validated quitter at 34-38 weeks, similar to a standard look-up value of £1390 per quitter. question: Do Wound Cultures Give Information About the Microbiology of Blood Cultures in Severe Burn Patients?
answer: In a retrospective study of severe burn patients, wound cultures were informative about bloodstream pathogens: the same pathogen was transmitted from wound to blood in 30% of all patients and in 65% of bacteremic patients. question: Could chest wall rigidity be a factor in rapid death from illicit fentanyl abuse?
answer: Post-mortem data from 48 fentanyl deaths suggest chest wall rigidity could contribute to rapid death: no appreciable norfentanyl was detected in 42% of cases, which the authors interpret as very rapid death consistent with acute chest rigidity. question: The Prevalence of Incidentally Detected Idiopathic Misty Mesentery on Multidetector Computed Tomography: Can Obesity Be the Triggering Cause?
answer: Isolated incidental idiopathic misty mesentery was found in 7% (80/561) of patients with misty mesentery on abdominopelvic CT, and most of these patients were obese (67.5%) or overweight (17.5%), which is compatible with obesity being a possible triggering factor.

question: Does Viral Co-Infection Influence the Severity of Acute Respiratory Infection in Children?
answer: In a prospective Spanish multicenter cohort of 204 children admitted with acute respiratory infection, the number of detected viruses did not correlate with any marker of severity; this was checked against a UK replication cohort of 97 children. question: Do risk calculators accurately predict surgical site occurrences?
answer: Existing risk models for surgical site occurrence after open ventral hernia repair showed poor predictive accuracy. question: Are serum leptin levels a prognostic factor in advanced lung cancer?
answer: In 71 previously untreated lung cancer patients, serum leptin levels showed no association with overall survival, so leptin was not a prognostic factor in this study.
